main_damage_causes: Complete omission of Sirius Black's only Book 1 appearance, eliminating his established presence as a trusted inner-circle ally on the night Voldemort fell
Loss of the Sirius-Hagrid relationship foundation, which the book seeds from page one by having Sirius trust Hagrid with his motorcycle
Absence of any early audience orientation toward Sirius as a named, loyal figure — his later prominence in Film 3 arrives without the subtle foreshadowing the book carefully plants
Sirius Black does not appear in either the book corpus or the film corpus provided — both corpora cover Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, in which Sirius Black plays no role
No book baseline for Sirius Black exists in the provided corpus, so no divergence can be evidenced

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Opening at Privet Drive: Hagrid delivers Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 8/13: Hagrid explicitly mentions 'Young Sirius Black lent it to me' (the motorcycle), establishing Sirius as a trusted, named ally of the Order from the very first chapter. Hagrid also says he'll be 'takin' Sirius his bike back,' reinforcing Sirius as an active, present figure in the wizarding world on this night.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits any mention of Sirius Black entirely. Hagrid arrives on the motorcycle with no attribution of its owner. Sirius's name, his trust relationship with Hagrid, and his implicit presence in the events of that night are completely erased from the adaptation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius Black's only appearance in Book 1 is this brief but meaningful mention — he lent Hagrid his motorcycle on the night Voldemort fell, placing him squarely among the inner circle of trusted allies. The film's omission removes the earliest seed of Sirius's character: his loyalty, his closeness to Hagrid and Dumbledore, and his active role on the most important night in wizarding history. For an audience encountering these films without the books, Sirius is introduced with zero prior context when he becomes plot-relevant in Film 3. The relationship between Sirius and the core group (Hagrid especially) loses its established foundation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Lupin's entrance and greeting of Black
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Lupin enters urgently, disarms everyone including Harry, then after a moment of staring at Black, embraces him. The reunion is wordless and charged. Lupin's opening line is 'Where is he, Sirius?' — immediately focused on Pettigrew, not on Black himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin enters and immediately delivers a taunting, almost contemptuous line: 'Looking a bit ragged, aren't we, Sirius? Finally the skin reflects the madness within.' Black responds in kind. The exchange frames them as adversaries before the embrace, and Lupin's first impulse reads as mockery rather than tension born of twelve years of grief and suspicion.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's reunion is wordless and devastating — Lupin embraces Black like a brother without explanation, shocking the trio. The film replaces this with witty banter that undercuts the emotional gravity of two men reuniting after twelve years of separation, false accusation, and Azkaban. The relationship dynamic is made to feel lighter and more performative than the book's raw, complicated grief.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's 'He dies. Now.' and 'I did my waiting!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Black is driven and dangerous in the Shrieking Shack but is also specific and coherent: he is fixed on Pettigrew, not on theatrical declarations. His urgency is about catching a traitor before he escapes again. When Lupin says they need to explain, Black accepts this ('All right, then'). His famous 'twelve years' line does not appear in the book in this form.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Black delivers the line 'I did my waiting! Twelve years of it! In Azkaban! Trust me, you wouldn't have lasted a week!' as a theatrical, almost villainous declaration of impatience. He is portrayed as barely controllable, lurching toward murderous action over Lupin's reasonable objections.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's most famous Black line ('I did my waiting!') reads as unhinged bravado rather than the book's controlled, purposeful urgency. It confirms the children's — and audience's — worst fears about Black's mental state at exactly the moment the film should begin casting doubt on those fears. It makes him harder to re-evaluate as innocent, weakening the pivot toward sympathy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Three Broomsticks) — Rosmerta challenges the narrative; McGonagall reveals godfather status
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes a full, detailed account: Black was Secret-Keeper by James's own choice (overriding Dumbledore's warnings), Pettigrew confronted Black publicly, Black laughed at the carnage. The overheard conversation is the primary vehicle by which Harry (and the reader) constructs a hatred of Black. Crucially, the book version of this scene gives McGonagall a line about Black and Potter being 'Ringleaders' and 'exceptionally bright,' and Flitwick says they were 'like brothers.' The emotional weight is built through detail.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the Three Broomsticks scene significantly. Rosmerta's challenge ('Of all the boys I ran out of here, Black's the last who would've gone over to the dark side. Hearsay. That's all the Ministry had. Hearsay.') is present but the rich backstory — the Fidelius Charm explanation, Hagrid's account of Black handing over the motorbike, the full portrait of their Hogwarts friendship — is mostly absent. The scene ends on the godfather revelation rather than building a complete picture of betrayal and friendship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Three Broomsticks scene is the emotional and expository centerpiece that makes the eventual revelation of Black's innocence so devastating. By compressing it, the film loses the detailed portrait of James-Sirius friendship that makes Harry's hatred feel earned and the truth feel like a genuine gut-punch. Rosmerta's 'hearsay' challenge is present but not given room to breathe — in the book it seeds doubt more effectively because it comes after the full weight of the accusation has been established.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Three Broomsticks) — Harry's reaction outside: 'I'm going to kill him'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Harry overhears the conversation and reacts with 'a hatred such as he had never known before coursing through him like poison.' But his inner monologue is more ambivalent — he doesn't know what he wants to do. He explicitly thinks he doesn't want to kill Black, just that doing nothing is unbearable. He tells Ron and Hermione 'I don't know what I want to do.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Harry, after overhearing the conversation, declares directly to Hermione: 'I hope he finds me. But when he does, I'm going to be ready. When he does, I'm going to kill him.' This is a direct, stated intention to murder.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Harry is consumed by rage but morally uncertain — which makes his later decision to spare Pettigrew (and implicitly Black) more coherent as a character arc. The film Harry explicitly states murderous intent, which makes his Shrieking Shack mercy feel less like a hard-won moral choice and more like a simple change of heart. It also makes Harry harder to sympathize with in the interim.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 22 (Gryffindor Common Room after second break-in) — 'I could've killed him'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Harry's response after Black's second break-in is not to fixate on a missed killing opportunity. He wonders why Black fled instead of killing Ron and proceeding to Harry, and thinks practically about what Black's escape route must have been. His emotional response is present but not centered on regret at failing to kill.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Harry stares out the window and says 'I could've killed him. He was right there. Close enough to touch. I could've killed him.' twice, with quiet, ominous intensity — as if he regrets not having murdered Black.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This moment amplifies Harry's murderous fixation in a way the book does not. It reinforces the film's pattern of making Harry's hatred more explicitly violent, which misrepresents his book characterization as someone consumed by rage but not coldly plotting murder.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's explanation of how he found Pettigrew
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Black gives a detailed and emotional account: he saw Pettigrew in the Daily Prophet photo (Fudge gave him the paper in Azkaban), recognized him at once, and explains that Pettigrew's survival meant he was waiting to deliver Harry to Voldemort when the time was right. Black's speech includes his reasoning about Pettigrew's cowardice and his own moral argument: 'THEN YOU SHOULD HAVE DIED! DIED RATHER THAN BETRAY YOUR FRIENDS, AS WE WOULD HAVE DONE FOR YOU!' This is a full moral indictment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses Black's explanation and the confrontation with Pettigrew. The key moral speech — about dying rather than betraying friends — is reduced to a single line: 'Died! Died rather than betray my friends!' without the full context of Pettigrew's year-long spying established in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Black's moral authority in the confrontation scene — his ability to articulate what courage and loyalty actually demand — is one of his defining character moments. The compression loses the full force of his indictment and reduces what should be a thematic centerpiece to a single line.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Absence of Black's account of how he persuaded the Potters to switch Secret-Keepers
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Black confesses: 'I persuaded Lily and James to change to Peter at the last moment, persuaded them to use him as Secret-Keeper instead of me... I'm to blame, I know it.' This is a devastating moment of self-recrimination — Black accepts moral responsibility even while being technically innocent of betrayal. It is the key beat that makes him a complex, genuinely tragic figure rather than simply a wronged innocent.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include Black's confession of his role in convincing the Potters to switch Secret-Keepers. He simply asserts 'It's a lie! I never would've betrayed James and Lily!' without the nuance of his actual guilt — the guilt of having been too clever, of thinking Pettigrew would be a safer decoy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most important piece of Black's characterization in the book. He is not merely an innocent victim of circumstance — he is a man who made a fateful mistake born of love and misplaced cunning, and he has carried that guilt for twelve years. Without this confession, film Black is a simpler wronged-man figure. The moral complexity — innocent of betrayal but responsible for the conditions that led to it — is entirely lost, significantly damaging his arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's account of how he escaped Azkaban via Animagus transformation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Black gives a full, emotionally rich account: 'I think the only reason I never lost my mind is that I knew I was innocent. That wasn't a happy thought, so the dementors couldn't suck it out of me... but it kept me sane... When it all became too much... I could transform in my cell... become a dog.' He explains how seeing Pettigrew in the paper gave him an obsessive purpose that cleared his mind and allowed him to slip out as a dog.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits Black's explanation of how he maintained his sanity in Azkaban and how he escaped. His inner psychological state during twelve years of imprisonment — the one happy-adjacent thought that sustained him — is never shared with Harry or the audience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Black's Azkaban survival story is central to understanding him: his innocence was itself the psychological anchor that the dementors couldn't strip away. This reveals something profound about him — and about the nature of innocence versus guilt — that the film entirely omits. It also establishes why Harry eventually believes him ('And at long last, Harry believed him'). The film's Harry has less reason to arrive at that belief organically.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 30 (Outside Whomping Willow) — Black invites Harry to live with him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book presents this scene in the tunnel, with Black nervous and halting: 'I'll understand, of course, if you want to stay with your aunt and uncle. But... well... think about it. Once my name's cleared... if you wanted a... a different home...' Harry's reaction is explosive joy: 'Are you insane? Of course I want to leave the Dursleys!' Black's face breaks into 'the first true smile Harry had seen upon it' — a moment of profound emotional release that makes him briefly look like his younger self.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes this scene but compresses it and relocates it to outside the Whomping Willow. The emotional texture is present but briefer. The book's specific detail — 'the first true smile,' the comparison to the wedding photograph — which makes this a genuine character revelation, is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's guardian offer scene is a rare moment where Black's humanity and the possibility of a restored future fully surface. The film gets the content but loses the emotional precision — particularly the transformation of Black's face — that makes it land as a character moment rather than a plot beat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 41 (Rooftop farewell) — Black's parting speech to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Black's final words before flying off on Buckbeak are: 'We'll see each other again. You are — truly your father's son, Harry.' Brief, emotional, forward-looking. His letter to Harry later establishes that he sent the Firebolt and provides the Hogsmeade permission note — acts of concrete, practical godfathering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Black delivers an extended, somewhat sentimental farewell speech: 'Trust yourself. No matter the challenges you face — and I fear they will be many — you'll be surprised how many times you can find the answers... here.' (tapping his heart). This is generic inspirational dialogue with no specific connection to Black's character or his relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film replaces Black's characteristically restrained, specific farewell with a generic 'trust your heart' speech that sounds like it belongs to any mentor figure. Book Black's voice is sharp, loving, and particular — he speaks to Harry as James's son, not as a generic young hero. The film's farewell substitutes sentiment for character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 30 (Whomping Willow exterior) — Black's attempt to comfort Lupin during transformation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book does not include a scene where Black attempts to talk Lupin down from transforming. In the book, Black simply says 'Run' and transforms immediately to battle the werewolf, protecting the children at risk to himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film adds a scene where Black wraps his arms around transforming Lupin and speaks to him: 'You know the man you truly are, Remus. This flesh is only flesh. This heart is where you truly live. This heart! Here!' — pounding Lupin's chest.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this is an addition rather than a removal, it characterizes Black in a somewhat uncharacteristically lyrical and therapeutic way. The book Black is defined by action, loyalty, and a certain blunt directness — not by quasi-mystical speeches about the soul. This is a minor voice inconsistency but the scene itself is not deeply damaging.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Three Broomsticks) — Absence of full Fidelius Charm explanation and friendship portrait
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book's Three Broomsticks scene includes Flitwick explaining the Fidelius Charm in detail, and crucially includes: 'You'd have thought Black and Potter were brothers!' (Flitwick), 'Both very bright, of course — exceptionally bright, in fact' (McGonagall), and Hagrid's story of Black at Godric's Hollow handing over the motorbike ('Give Harry ter me, Hagrid, I'm his godfather, I'll look after him'). These details build a full picture of who Black was before — making the betrayal more devastating and the truth more poignant.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits Hagrid's account of meeting Black at Godric's Hollow, the detailed description of Black and Potter's friendship as 'like brothers,' and the Fidelius Charm mechanics. The scene goes from 'Black told You-Know-Who' to 'Pettigrew confronted Black' to 'Black's the godfather' without the intervening texture.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The portrait of pre-Azkaban Black — brilliant, devoted, inseparable from James — is what gives his story its tragic dimension. Without Hagrid's account of Black at Godric's Hollow (white and shaking, handing over the motorbike, saying 'I won't need it anymore'), the audience never fully grasps what Black lost, what he gave up, or the scope of Pettigrew's betrayal. This compression reduces Black from a tragic figure to a plot mechanism.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2-3: Sirius's head-in-fire meeting with Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes a rich, multi-layered conversation: Sirius is warm and caring, lets Harry talk himself out before speaking, shows concern ('eyes full of concern'), provides detailed strategic intelligence about Karkaroff's Death Eater history, warns about Moody's attack, analyzes the Dark Mark situation, and crucially begins to give Harry specific tactical advice about how to survive the dragon task before being interrupted. He is proactive, analytical, and deeply engaged as both godfather and strategic advisor.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the meeting into a brief, urgent exchange focused almost entirely on warning Harry that 'the devils are inside the walls,' identifying Karkaroff as a Death Eater, and mentioning Crouch. Sirius gives no dragon advice, no detailed strategic analysis, no warmth or personal connection beyond the functional. His closing line is 'Keep your friends close, Harry' — a generic platitude. He is primarily a delivery mechanism for plot exposition rather than a fully realized godfather figure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's fireplace scene is one of the most important Sirius moments in Goblet of Fire: it establishes him as Harry's primary emotional anchor, a brilliant strategic mind, and a caring godfather who risks his freedom to help. The film strips this down to a plot-delivery scene. Sirius loses his analytical depth, his warmth, his tactical agency (dragon advice never given), and his emotional attunement. The relationship dimension — Harry's desperate need for a parent-figure — is almost entirely absent. 'Keep your friends close' replaces pages of nuanced, emotionally resonant guidance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2: Sirius's letter delivered by owl — voice-over format
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Sirius's letter as written communication, with Sirius instructing Harry to keep changing owls, stay alert, and not forget about the scar — practical, protective advice delivered in a written voice that reflects his character. Harry's careful reading of and emotional response to the letter (rolling it up, feeling reassured by Sirius's proximity) is part of the texture of their correspondence relationship.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The letter is delivered as a spoken voice-over with Sirius narrating directly to Harry, including a jokey postscript about the bird biting ('P.S. The bird bites'). This transforms a serious, careful communication into something lighter and more casual, and collapses the epistolary relationship into a single shorthand moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book builds Sirius's relationship with Harry substantially through their correspondence — multiple letters, Harry's anxiety waiting for replies, his relief at hearing Sirius is close. The film reduces this to a single voice-over with a comic coda. The jokey 'the bird bites' undercuts the tone of urgency and care Sirius maintains throughout their communication in the books. While minor in isolation, it contributes to a pattern of softening the depth and stakes of the godfather relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3: Sirius disappears from fire when Ron enters
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that after Ron interrupts and Harry scrambles to hide the fireplace, Sirius has already popped away ('He heard a tiny pop! in the fire behind him and knew Sirius had gone'). Harry's anguish is that Sirius was cut off before finishing his dragon advice — 'Who had decided to go for a stroll at one o'clock in the morning, and stopped Sirius from telling him how to get past a dragon?' Harry feels responsible and guilty. Sirius had been mid-sentence about a 'simple spell.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: When Ron enters, Harry turns away from the fire and goes to meet Ron. When Harry returns to the fire, Sirius is gone — but the film has already had Sirius give his complete message ('Keep your friends close'). There is no interrupted advice, no dramatic irony, no sense of loss. Harry does not appear troubled by Sirius's departure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, the interruption of Sirius mid-advice is dramatically crucial: it creates tension (Harry doesn't know how to face the dragon), it makes the subsequent research with Hermione urgent, and it makes Hagrid's tip and the Summoning Charm solution feel earned. The film removes this entirely because Sirius has nothing more to say anyway. This is downstream damage from the compression of the fireplace scene, but it independently removes a key structural beat: Sirius as the source of interrupted but vital agency for Harry's survival.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3: Sirius's characterization of Karkaroff and Crouch
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book gives Sirius an extended, nuanced analysis of both Karkaroff (detailed history as a Death Eater who named names to escape Azkaban, was in Azkaban with Sirius, teaching Dark Arts at Durmstrang) and Crouch (sent Sirius to Azkaban without trial, rose to power through harsh measures, gave his own son to the dementors, the tragic backstory of Crouch Jr.). Sirius speaks with personal knowledge, bitterness, and moral complexity — this is information only he can provide and it establishes him as uniquely positioned to understand the wizarding world's dark history.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Sirius reduces Karkaroff to 'He was a Death Eater. And no one, no one stops being a Death Eater' and Crouch to 'Heart of stone. Sent his own son to Azkaban.' These are declarative plot-summary lines with no texture, no personal history, no moral complexity. The tragic Crouch Jr. backstory — which Sirius tells with grim detail in the book, including watching the boy scream through his cell door — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's cave scene (and the fireplace scene's Karkaroff analysis) establishes Sirius as a man shaped by direct experience of Azkaban's horrors, capable of empathy even for enemies (Crouch Jr.), and possessed of unique insider knowledge. The film's reductive summaries strip him of this depth and make him sound like a plot-delivery device rather than a fully realised character with a painful past informing his judgments. The loss of the Crouch Jr. story in particular removes one of Sirius's most powerful moments of morally complex testimony.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film: Entire cave/Hogsmeade meeting with Harry, Ron, Hermione absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book contains a long, richly detailed scene in which Sirius meets Harry, Ron, and Hermione in a cave near Hogsmeade. He is thin and living off rats, gnawing chicken bones 'in a very doglike way,' grinning at Harry despite his hardship. He conducts a full investigative analysis of the Winky/Dark Mark/Crouch situation, paces the cave thinking aloud, quotes 'If you want to know what a man's like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors,' interrogates the group methodically, draws insightful conclusions about Crouch's absences, and gives protective instructions ('don't leave Hogwarts,' 'call me Snuffles'). He is simultaneously physically diminished and intellectually formidable — a complex, memorable portrait.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no cave scene. This entire sequence — Sirius's physical presence, his investigative brilliance, his moral insights, his care for Harry's safety, his relationship with Ron and Hermione, his living conditions as a fugitive — is absent from the film corpus provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cave scene is the single most important Sirius scene in Goblet of Fire in terms of characterization. It shows him as Harry's protector willing to suffer hardship, a brilliant analyst of Ministry corruption, a moral voice ('how he treats his inferiors'), and an emotionally present godfather. Without it, Sirius's role in the film is reduced to a face in a fire delivering warnings. His agency, his intelligence, his relationship with all three protagonists, and his physical reality as a fugitive are all lost. This is the primary source of structural damage to his portrayal in this film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5/6: Sirius absent from Dumbledore's office post-tournament climax
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has Sirius physically present in Dumbledore's office after the third task. He crosses the room swiftly when Harry enters ('In one swift moment, he had crossed the room'), his hands shaking as he helps Harry into a chair, asking urgently 'Harry, are you all right?' He advocates for Harry ('We can leave that till morning, can't we, Dumbledore? Let him have a sleep'), grips Harry's shoulder throughout the debriefing (sometimes painfully), covers his face with his hands at the horror of Harry's account, and finally receives Dumbledore's mission to alert the Order. Harry explicitly 'wanted Sirius to stay' and feels grief at his departure. Sirius transforms into the dog and walks Harry to the hospital wing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain the post-climax Dumbledore's office scene with Sirius present. The corpus ends before this point in the narrative (the final Dumbledore's office material in the film corpus concerns the Pensieve/Barty Jr. reveal). Sirius's physical presence at Harry's most traumatic moment, his emotional support, his active participation in the post-Voldemort debrief, and his farewell to Harry are absent from the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The post-climax scene is the emotional culmination of the Sirius-Harry relationship in this book. Sirius being physically there — shaking, gripping Harry's shoulder, covering his face — is the payoff for an entire book of dangerous correspondence and sacrifice. His advocacy for Harry ('let him rest'), his visible distress, and his reluctant departure on Dumbledore's orders all demonstrate his love and his function as Harry's surrogate parent. The absence of this scene from the film corpus means the relationship's emotional arc has no resolution in the film, and Harry's trauma is not witnessed by the one person whose presence would matter most.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1: Harry writes 'Sirius Black' on letter cover — no internal monologue establishing emotional need
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes with great care Harry's realisation that he needs Sirius: 'What he really wanted (and it felt almost shameful to admit it to himself) was someone like - someone like a parent: an adult wizard whose advice he could ask without feeling stupid, someone who cared about him.' The solution ('It was so simple, and so obvious... Sirius') comes with wonder that he hadn't thought of it immediately, and the explanation of why — he'd only known about Sirius for two months. This establishes the emotional foundation of the entire godfather relationship in GoF.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Harry writing 'Sirius Black' on a letter after Hermione prompts him ('You know Sirius will want to hear about this'). There is no internal process, no sense of Harry reaching for a parent-figure, no emotional weight to the act. It is Hermione's suggestion, not Harry's independent realisation of his need.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's moment of Harry realising he needs Sirius is foundational to the entire godfather subplot's emotional logic — it tells the audience why this relationship matters so much. By having Hermione prompt the contact instead, the film transfers Harry's agency to Hermione and loses the crucial insight that Sirius fills a parental void for Harry. This makes the relationship feel more functional (information exchange) than emotional (surrogate family), which diminishes every subsequent Sirius scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – King's Cross platform farewell
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 332–337: Sirius transforms into the dog and accompanies Harry to King's Cross, bounding alongside the train, chasing pigeons, scaring cats for Harry's entertainment. He rears up on hind legs to place paws on Harry's shoulders before Mrs Weasley shoves Harry toward the train. The scene is joyful and bittersweet, showing Sirius desperate for connection and savoring rare freedom, bounded by risk.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Moody scolds Sirius ('Padfoot, are you barking mad? You'll blow the entire operation'), and Sirius defends himself with 'What's life without a little risk?' He then sits with Harry privately, gives him the Order of the Phoenix photograph, and delivers sentimental exposition about Neville's parents and James. The dog-form pursuit of the train, the playful animal behavior, and the bittersweet farewell through the window are absent. The scene is reframed as a calm information-delivery and emotional statement rather than a reckless act of love.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's platform scene conveys Sirius's character through action: he is reckless not out of carelessness but out of desperate need for connection and a refusal to be entirely extinguished. The film replaces this with dialogue that tells us he is reckless ('What's life without a little risk?') while actually showing him sitting calmly. The loss of the dog bounding alongside the train—one of the most affective images of Sirius's imprisonment and love for Harry—flattens the emotional register. Moody's scolding reframes the moment as an operational blunder rather than a characterful act of devotion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Sirius's photograph/exposition scene at King's Cross
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 4–13, 56–61: Sirius's warmth for Harry is established through ongoing letters, small gestures, and the grimly sardonic humor of the kitchen reunion. His emotional depth and connection to James are shown organically across many scenes. He does not deliver set-piece emotional speeches to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Sirius hands Harry a photograph and delivers a speech: 'It's been 14 years and still a day doesn't go by I don't miss your dad.' This is the primary vehicle in the film for establishing Sirius's bond with James and his emotional interiority. It is a compressed, expository substitution for the distributed, organic characterization in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book builds Sirius's grief over James across multiple scenes—the tapestry conversation, the Pensieve discussion, the kitchen reunion—allowing the audience to feel rather than be told the depth of loss. The film condenses this into one expository speech, which reduces Sirius from a man carrying sustained grief to a man who delivers a grief monologue. The emotional weight is declared rather than earned.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Order briefing: Sirius's 'stronger and stronger by the minute' line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 132–160: Sirius leads the briefing of Harry calmly and with authority, relaying strategic information (Voldemort building his army, recruiting giants, seeking a weapon) with deliberate care. He is the primary explainer, measured and purposeful. He argues for Harry's right to know and wins partial ground. His manner is controlled, strategic, and adult.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Sirius is heard saying '...stronger and stronger by the minute! We have to act now' before Mrs Weasley shushes the meeting. In the subsequent kitchen scene he delivers fragments of information but shares the briefing heavily with Lupin and Moody, and his most prominent individual moment is the confrontation with Molly over Harry. His strategic competence and leadership within the Order are largely displaced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Sirius is the central authoritative voice of the Order briefing—Harry's primary conduit to understanding the war. In the film, this function is distributed among multiple characters and Sirius's visible contribution to Order strategy is minimal. The 'act now' fragment makes him sound impulsive rather than strategically engaged, reinforcing the film's reductive reading of Sirius as reckless rather than capable.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Snape's entrance and 'How touchingly paternal' exchange
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 640–675: The Snape/Sirius kitchen confrontation is an extended, tense scene. Sirius asserts his authority as homeowner, defends Harry as godfather, trades pointed insults with Snape about their shared history ('I've warned you, Snivelus'), and eventually has to be physically restrained by Harry and then calmed by the arrival of the Weasleys. Sirius is volatile but his protectiveness of Harry is the clear moral engine of the scene. His bitterness at being housebound and Snape's cruelty about it are both made explicit.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Snape delivers the line 'How touchingly paternal, Black. Perhaps Potter will grow up to be a felon, just like his godfather.' Sirius's response is abbreviated—'You stay out of this, Snivelus' and 'I know better'—and the confrontation is defused immediately. The full hostility, the drawn wands, the physical intervention by Harry, and Sirius's emotional exposure are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Snape/Sirius confrontation is one of the most important scenes for understanding Sirius's psychology: his rage at being trapped, his hatred of Snape rooted in genuine history, and his fierce if flawed protectiveness of Harry. Reducing it to a single exchange of epithets loses the insight into how deeply Sirius is damaged by his confinement and how that damage manifests. It also loses the book's nuance that Sirius is simultaneously right (he does know better about Snape) and dangerously volatile.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Sirius in the fire, fireplace conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 396–440, 476–513, 817–842: Sirius appears in the Gryffindor fire on multiple occasions. These scenes establish his loneliness ('it's just been Kreacher and me here'), his sharp political intelligence (explaining Fudge's paranoia, Umbridge's anti-werewolf legislation), his enthusiasm for the DA, his hurt when Harry declines his visit to Hogsmeade ('You're less like your father than I thought'), and in the final fire scene his deeply moving response to Harry's questions about James—admitting fault, showing genuine reflection, and demonstrating the complexity of his friendship with James.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: There is a single composite fire scene. Sirius tells Harry that Fudge doesn't want students trained in combat and that Voldemort is recruiting. The nuanced political analysis, the loneliness, the Hogsmeade offer and wounded comparison to James, the Umbridge/werewolf legislation insight, and the extended Pensieve-aftermath conversation about James's character are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's fire scenes are the primary means by which the audience understands Sirius as an isolated, intelligent, emotionally complex man rather than a plot device. His loneliness ('just been Kreacher and me'), his wounded pride when Harry rejects his visit, his self-aware admission that he was 'an arrogant little berk' at fifteen—all of this is lost. The film Sirius exists primarily as a supportive presence and source of intelligence, not as a fully realized person whose death carries maximum weight.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Sirius's comment 'Nice one, James!' during the Department of Mysteries battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 1004: Sirius shouts 'Nice one!' to Harry during the battle and tells him to get out. There is no 'James' in the book. Sirius is fully present in the moment, fighting alongside Harry and concerned for his safety.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Sirius calls Harry 'James' during the battle ('Nice one, James!'). This is the film's single most explicit confirmation of Mrs Weasley's accusation that Sirius confuses Harry with his dead father.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Dumbledore explicitly tells Harry that Sirius was 'brave, clever and energetic' and Mrs Weasley's accusation is contested. The book allows the reader to weigh whether Sirius truly confuses Harry with James or whether Molly is projecting. The film resolves this ambiguity by having Sirius literally call Harry 'James' in an unguarded moment. This decisively frames Sirius's love for Harry as pathological displacement rather than genuine independent attachment, which damages both the relationship and Sirius's psychological coherence as a character. It also retroactively colors every warm moment between them.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Harry/Sirius Christmas conversation about the snake vision
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 589–598: Harry privately tells Sirius about his vision of being the snake and his fear that he is becoming Voldemort. Sirius's response is inadequate—he dismisses it as aftermath of the vision and tells Harry to sleep—but he is clearly shaken. The scene establishes Sirius's limits as a guardian: he cannot fully engage with Harry's darkest fears, whether from emotional limitation or an inability to face that Harry might be in genuine danger. This is a specific, honest character flaw.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Harry's equivalent confession ('what if I'm becoming bad?') is directed at Sirius in his room at Grimmauld Place. Sirius responds warmly and reassuringly ('You are not becoming Voldemort, Harry'), with no trace of the inadequacy or shaken quality present in the book. The scene is brief and affirming.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book version of this scene is important because it shows Sirius's genuine flaw as a godfather: he is not equipped to handle Harry's deepest fears, and his inadequacy here is part of why Harry does not fully confide in him later. The film turns it into a straightforward reassurance scene, removing the honest complexity of their relationship and making Sirius a simpler supportive figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Sirius's death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 1010–1029: Sirius is laughing as he duels Bellatrix—'Come on, you can do better than that!'—and is struck mid-laugh, his expression shifting from laughter to shock. He falls in a 'graceful arc' through the veil. Harry's denial is prolonged and agonized, rooted in his inability to accept finality: Sirius always came back before, always risked everything to be there. Lupin physically restrains Harry. The scene is the emotional climax of the entire novel.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Sirius is struck by Bellatrix's 'Avada Kedavra' and falls backward through the veil. The moment is visually rendered but the laughter—the defining character detail of how Sirius meets death—is absent from the corpus evidence provided. Lupin restrains Harry briefly. The scene is present but compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's detail that Sirius is laughing when he dies is not incidental—it is the crystallization of his entire character: defiant, alive, refusing to be diminished even at the moment of death. It is also what makes the moment land so hard for Harry, who cannot reconcile the laughing man with someone who could simply be gone. The absence of this specific detail from the filmed death reduces the scene from a characterful tragedy to a functional plot event.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Near-total absence of Sirius's isolation and depression at Grimmauld Place
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 80–91, 290–296, 545, 636–638: Sirius's deterioration at Grimmauld Place is extensively documented. After Harry returns to Hogwarts, Sirius becomes 'moodier and surlier than before,' withdraws to Buckbeak's room, and his 'gloom seeped through the house, oozing under doorways like some noxious gas.' Harry cannot leave for Hogwarts without worrying Snape's taunts will push Sirius to something rash. Sirius is described as only recovering his spirits during Christmas. This arc is central to understanding why he ultimately goes to the Department of Mysteries.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film: Sirius's post-summer isolation and progressive deterioration are absent. The film shows him at Christmas in good spirits and in the fire conversation providing intelligence. There is no portrayal of his psychological decline, his withdrawal, or the dangerous restlessness that makes his eventual decision to come to the Ministry psychologically motivated rather than arbitrary.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's most important contribution to Sirius's arc is the extended portrayal of what Grimmauld Place does to him—how it erodes the man who survived Azkaban by turning freedom into a different kind of prison. This is the psychological cause of his death: he goes to the Ministry not just because Harry calls but because he has been slowly broken by confinement. Without this arc, his death is an arbitrary plot event rather than the tragic culmination of a year of slow suffocation. The film loses the thematic through-line connecting imprisonment, identity, and sacrifice.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Absence of the Kreacher/Sirius dynamic and its consequences
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 187–203, 248–252, 628–635, 1060–1076: Sirius's treatment of Kreacher is an extended moral theme. Sirius dismisses Kreacher as beneath notice ('a foul little...'), threatens him, throws him out of rooms, and refuses to engage with Hermione's arguments for treating him with respect. Dumbledore later tells Harry explicitly that 'Sirius did nothing to make Kreacher's lot easier' and that this contributed directly to Kreacher betraying him to the Malfoys, which enabled Voldemort's trap and Sirius's death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Kreacher appears briefly at Christmas. Sirius dismisses him ('That's enough of your bile. Away with you') and makes a brief comment about him not being pleasant even when Sirius was a boy. There is no extended portrayal of the moral failure, no Hermione counter-argument shown in depth, and no later reckoning with the consequences.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Sirius/Kreacher dynamic is one of the book's most carefully constructed moral arguments: Sirius's failure of compassion toward Kreacher is not presented as villainous but as a specific, comprehensible flaw rooted in his history with the Black family, and it has direct fatal consequences. It also prefigures the house-elf liberation theme that pays off in later books. The film reduces Kreacher to brief comic grotesquerie, losing the causal chain that makes Sirius's death a tragedy of character rather than bad luck, and losing Sirius's moral complexity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Absence of the two-way mirror gift and its tragic irony
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 682–685, 1116–1126: Before Harry leaves Grimmauld Place after Christmas, Sirius gives him a badly wrapped package containing a two-way mirror, explaining that Harry can use it to contact him if Snape gives him trouble. Harry decides he will never use it because he will not lure Sirius from safety. After Sirius's death, Harry finds the package unopened, uses the mirror, and Sirius does not answer. The mirror is a symbol of the connection they never fully used and now never can.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film: The two-way mirror is entirely absent from the film corpus provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The two-way mirror is not a minor detail. It is the emotional keystone of the Harry/Sirius relationship's tragic arc: Sirius offers a tool of connection; Harry refuses to use it out of misguided protectiveness; Sirius dies; Harry finds the mirror too late. This sequence is one of the book's most devastating ironies—Harry's love for Sirius was expressed as protection and ended up as the thing that prevented him from knowing Sirius was safe. Without the mirror, the audience loses the full weight of what Harry has lost and the specific mechanism of his guilt. It also removes one of the book's most powerful arguments about the cost of withheld communication.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slughorn's house / photograph shelf) - Slughorn references Sirius
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 47 establishes that Sirius was a Gryffindor, a talented boy Slughorn would have liked to have in his collection, and that he was a 'big pal' of James Potter's. Slughorn frames Sirius as a missed acquisition, a student of note. Book Scene 50 reinforces Sirius as a figure Harry measures sacrifice against — someone who lived on rats in a cave — giving him moral weight.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Slughorn points out Regulus Black's photograph and mentions Sirius only as Regulus's older brother who 'died a few weeks ago.' Harry picks up the photograph because the boy resembles Sirius. Sirius is reduced to a physical reference point and a recent death, with no mention of his friendship with James, his House, or his character. He exists only to anchor Regulus and to register Harry's grief visually.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this Slughorn moment to characterise Sirius as a figure of genuine distinction — talented, memorable, someone who broke the Black family mould by going to Gryffindor. The film collapses this into a throwaway death notice. For an audience whose primary knowledge of Sirius comes from the films, this forfeits one of the few post-mortem moments that affirms who Sirius was as a person rather than simply as a loss Harry is processing.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slughorn's house) - absence of Sirius-as-Gryffindor-rebel context
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 47: Slughorn explicitly notes that the entire Black family had been in his House (Slytherin) but Sirius ended up in Gryffindor, framing Sirius as an anomaly who defied his family's trajectory. This is characterisation that speaks directly to Sirius's independent nature and his bond with James.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits entirely the detail that Sirius broke from his family by being sorted into Gryffindor. Slughorn's line about wanting 'the set' (both Black brothers) is retained in spirit but without the Gryffindor/Slytherin dimension, removing the thematic resonance of Sirius's defiance of his blood.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Gryffindor detail is not decorative — it encapsulates Sirius's defining characteristic: choosing loyalty and courage over family expectation. Its absence means the film never delivers this posthumous affirmation of Sirius's identity, compounding the already thin characterisation he receives after his death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Dumbledore's conversation with Harry about Sirius (book equivalent of Scenes 52–57)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 52–57 contain Dumbledore's private conversation with Harry in the Weasleys' broomstick shed, in which Dumbledore explicitly honours Sirius: 'I think Sirius would have been proud of you'; 'It was cruel that you and Sirius had such a short time together. A brutal ending to what should have been a long and happy relationship'; and ultimately, 'Spoken both like your mother and father's son and Sirius's true godson!' Harry's grief is articulated — he speaks of Sirius 'almost like a parent' and the loss of letters — and Dumbledore validates Sirius's significance to Harry's identity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no equivalent scene. Dumbledore's first private meeting with Harry (Film Scene 3, the train platform) is brief and pivots immediately to collecting Slughorn. There is no moment where Dumbledore speaks about Sirius, validates Harry's grief, or frames Sirius as a parental figure whose loss is structurally meaningful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the scene that most fully articulates Sirius's role in Harry's emotional life — as a near-parent, as someone who wrote letters, as someone whose death Harry is actively processing rather than suppressing. Its absence means the audience never hears Dumbledore (the story's moral authority) confirm that Sirius mattered deeply and specifically to Harry's development. Harry's grief for Sirius becomes background texture rather than a named, validated arc, which damages the audience's understanding of what Sirius represented and diminishes the weight of his death across the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Sirius's will scene (book equivalent of Scenes 25–37)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 25–37 establish that Sirius left Harry everything: gold, Grimmauld Place, Kreacher, and Buckbeak. Harry's reaction to each bequest reveals his relationship with Sirius — he doesn't want the house because it reminds him of Sirius 'imprisoned within the place he had wanted so desperately to leave'; he is repulsed by owning Kreacher because Kreacher betrayed Sirius; he immediately wants Buckbeak to stay with Hagrid. These are active, characterising choices that show Sirius through Harry's memory and grief.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no will scene. There is no reference to Harry inheriting from Sirius, no Kreacher scene, no discussion of Grimmauld Place's ownership. Buckbeak appears briefly (Film Scene 18 context, Hagrid's hut) but without any connection to Sirius's bequest.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The will scene is the primary mechanism by which Sirius continues to act in the story after his death — his choices (what he owned, who he trusted, what he left behind) shape Harry's circumstances and reveal his character. Its omission removes Sirius's posthumous agency entirely and also eliminates the Kreacher plot thread that has consequences later in the saga. For this film specifically, it means Sirius's death has no narrative ripple beyond Harry's emotional state.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Dumbledore's death / courtyard) — Ginny comforts Harry, Sirius context absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 279: Harry reflects that 'there had been no body to bury when Sirius had died' and contrasts his experience of Dumbledore's death with the unresolved nature of Sirius's — noting he had not, as with Sirius, looked desperately for a loophole. This comparison gives Sirius's death continued psychological presence and distinguishes the two losses in Harry's interior life.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's equivalent scene (Film Scene 19) focuses on Harry weeping over Dumbledore's body with Ginny comforting him. There is no interior reflection, no comparison to Sirius's death, no acknowledgement that Harry is now processing a second devastating loss of a father figure. Sirius is entirely absent from this moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book deliberately links these two losses — Sirius and Dumbledore — as part of Harry's accumulating grief over father figures. The film's omission of this connection means Sirius's death is not given the retrospective weight the narrative intends. The two losses remain isolated rather than forming a pattern that defines Harry's orphaned emotional trajectory.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Snape detention scene with James and Sirius's records (book equivalent of Scenes 218–220)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 218–220: Snape assigns Harry to sort through detention records and specifically shows Harry the card for 'James Potter and Sirius Black — Apprehended using an illegal hex upon Bertram Aubrey. Aubrey's head twice normal size. Double detention.' Harry reads through their various offences, Sirius and James consistently coupled together in misdeeds, alongside Lupin and Pettigrew. Snape uses this deliberately to wound Harry. The scene characterises Sirius as a mischievous, bold, loyal friend — and as someone whose memory Snape actively weaponises.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no detention scene of this kind. Snape's cruelty toward Harry regarding Sirius's memory is not dramatised through this mechanism.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene does double work: it gives Sirius continued characterisation as a specific, vivid person (a rule-breaker, James's co-conspirator) and it establishes Snape's particular malice regarding Sirius's memory. Its loss means one of the few scenes where Sirius is characterised through action rather than grief is missing, and Snape's relationship to Sirius's legacy is less textured.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Harry's reflection on Snape's taunts contributing to Sirius's death (book Scene 105–106)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 105–106: Harry explicitly reflects that Snape's snide remarks to Sirius about 'remaining safely hidden while the rest of the Order were off fighting' had probably been 'a powerful factor in Sirius rushing off to the Ministry the night that he had died.' Harry clings to this because it lets him blame Snape. This is a rare moment of Harry processing the causality of Sirius's death and gives Sirius's fatal decision — going to the Ministry — a psychological backstory rooted in his wounded pride.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no equivalent internal reflection. Harry's rage at Snape on the grounds after Dumbledore's death (Film Scene 18) is pure reactive fury with no reference to Sirius or the history between Snape and Sirius.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book passage explains why Sirius died the way he did — not just that Bellatrix killed him, but that his own impulsive pride, stoked by Snape's mockery, drove him into the open. This humanises Sirius's fatal flaw and gives his death tragic coherence. Its absence leaves Sirius's death as an unexplained event from a prior film rather than something with psychological roots the audience can understand.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Mundungus stealing Sirius's possessions scene (book equivalent of Scenes 133–140)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 133–140: Harry confronts Mundungus Fletcher for stealing items from Sirius's house, including objects bearing the Black family crest. Harry is furious — 'He's nicked Sirius's stuff! Nicked it!' — and the scene establishes both Harry's protectiveness of Sirius's memory and the practical reality of the inheritance. Dumbledore later assures Harry that Mundungus will not take more.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Mundungus scene. There is no dramatisation of Harry protecting Sirius's legacy or of the Grimmauld Place inheritance.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While not structurally critical, this scene is one of the few in HBP where Harry actively defends Sirius's memory through action rather than passive grief. Its absence reduces Sirius to someone Harry mourns internally but never fights for.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Shell Cottage cliff) — Harry explains the mirror shard to Ron
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (DH ch.7/10), the mirror shard is a fragment of the two-way mirror Sirius gave Harry in OotP. Harry keeps it because it is one of the few remaining physical traces of Sirius; it is an object of grief and longing. He carries it in the mokeskin purse alongside the Marauder's Map and the fake locket — items he prizes. The shard later connects to Aberforth, but Harry never knows this during the horcrux hunt; he simply sees what he believes is Dumbledore's eye and is comforted/confused by it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 21 has Harry explicitly explain the mirror to Ron: 'Sirius gave it to me. He had a matching piece. He said if I ever needed him, all I had to do was look into it.' Harry then says he thinks he has seen Dumbledore in it. This compresses and distorts the emotional history of the object: in the books Harry never successfully used it while Sirius was alive and is haunted by that failure (Sirius died partly because Harry did not use the mirror instead of flying to the DoM). The film strips the guilt dimension entirely, recasting the shard as a straightforwardly useful communication tool Harry simply forgot to use, rather than a symbol of his failure and grief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius's gift of the mirror and Harry's failure to use it is a key node of Harry's guilt over Sirius's death. By presenting the mirror as something Harry just 'never got to use' without any guilt framing, the film loses the emotional weight Sirius's death carries into Deathly Hallows and weakens the ongoing cost of that loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sirius's room, Grimmauld Place) — Harry in the room
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.10 describes Sirius's room in rich detail: Gryffindor banners deliberately provocative toward his Slytherin family, Muggle motorcycle posters, posters of bikini-clad Muggle girls (stationary, proving they are Muggle), and crucially a photograph of the four Marauders — young, happy, 'carelessly handsome' Sirius with 'slightly arrogant face so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive.' Harry also finds Lily's letter to Sirius, searches desperately for the rest, and finds the torn photograph of baby Harry on a broomstick. The room establishes Sirius's personality, his rebelliousness, his deep friendship with James, and his bond with the Potters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 reduces the room visit to Harry briefly pausing at a photograph of the four Marauders at the Whomping Willow and finding Lily's letter on the floor. The Gryffindor banners, the Muggle girl posters (which signal Sirius's personality and his rebellion), the motorcycle posters, and the frantic search for the rest of the letter and the torn baby-Harry photograph are all absent. The room is just 'ransacked' with books scattered.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The bedroom is the primary corpus evidence for Sirius's youthful personality in DH — his wit, nerve, rebelliousness, love of Muggles, and defiant affection for James. Stripping it to a bare ransacked space removes almost all of this characterisation. The book's Sirius is vividly present in his room even in death; the film's version makes the room functionally inert.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Kitchen, Grimmauld Place) — Kreacher interrogation about the locket
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.10: Harry questions Kreacher at length. Kreacher tells the full story of being taken to the cave by Voldemort, drinking the potion, the Inferi, escaping via house-elf magic, and Regulus's subsequent heroic self-sacrifice. Harry watches Kreacher weep and is moved. Hermione explains that Sirius was 'horrible to Kreacher' and that Kreacher betrayed Sirius because Sirius never treated him as a being with feelings — a direct moral indictment of Sirius. Harry has 'no retort' and remembers Dumbledore's words: 'I do not think Sirius ever saw Kreacher as a being with feelings as acute as a human's.' Harry then shows Kreacher the fake locket as a gift, which transforms Kreacher's loyalty. The whole scene is a moral reckoning about how Sirius's cruelty contributed to his own death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 has Kreacher give only a brief, functional account: Regulus ordered him to destroy the locket, he could not, Mundungus took it. There is no account of the cave, no weeping, no Hermione speech about Sirius's cruelty, no moral reckoning. Harry simply orders Kreacher to find Mundungus and Kreacher vanishes. Ron grabs Kreacher by the neck and shakes him — the opposite of the book's moment of empathy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is the primary moment in DH where Sirius's moral failure is explicitly examined by other characters and by Harry himself. Its omission removes the only substantive critical perspective on Sirius in the book corpus, erases the causal link between Sirius's treatment of Kreacher and his death, and eliminates the thematic argument about how wizards' treatment of house-elves has consequences. Sirius's agency in his own death (via his cruelty) is completely lost, which distorts audience understanding of his character's flaws.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 23 (Hogsmeade/Aberforth's pub) — explanation of the mirror shard provenance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH: Aberforth has the twin mirror because Mundungus stole it from Grimmauld Place after Sirius's death. Harry is angry that Dung sold it — 'It belonged to Sirius.' This beat reaffirms the emotional significance of the mirror as Sirius's possession and Harry's continuing possessiveness of anything connected to his godfather.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 23 includes Aberforth saying 'Sirius. Albus told me.' and Harry saying 'Dung had no right selling you that. It belonged to —' which is faithful to that beat. However, the scene is brief and Harry's anger is quickly redirected. This scene is largely faithful and causes minimal damage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line is present and broadly faithful. Damage is minimal — Harry's emotional connection to Sirius's possessions is at least partially conveyed, though the depth of grief is not elaborated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Snape's memories — Great Hall sorting) — Sirius and James at Gryffindor table
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.33 ('The Prince's Tale'): At the sorting, Sirius nudges along the bench to make room for Lily when she is sorted into Gryffindor. Lily takes one look at him, 'seemed to recognise him from the train, folded her arms, and firmly turned her back on him.' This establishes that even as an eleven-year-old Sirius had already made a bad impression on Lily, consistent with his arrogance on the train. It also shows James's immediate attraction to Lily and Sirius's easy social dominance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 29 shows Sirius and James at the Gryffindor table watching the sorting. James nudges Sirius to move over and make space for Lily. Lily sits down and glances across at Snape. The beat of Lily recognising Sirius from the train and turning her back on him is absent. Sirius is a mostly silent background figure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book beat is small but establishes that Sirius's arrogance was apparent even to Lily from the very first moment at Hogwarts. Its absence is a minor omission but consistent with the film's overall pattern of smoothing Sirius's rougher edges.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 32 (Forbidden Forest) — Sirius with the Resurrection Stone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.34: Sirius appears via the Resurrection Stone. He is described as 'tall and handsome, and younger by far than Harry had ever seen him in life. He loped with an easy grace, his hands in his pockets and a grin on his face.' He tells Harry dying is 'Quicker and easier than falling asleep.' He says 'We are part of you. Invisible to anyone else.' His characterisation here is confident, warm, and physically graceful — his youth and ease restored. He is also specifically Sirius, with his own voice and bearing distinct from James or Lupin.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 32 shows Sirius (as Sirius Black) appearing with James, Lupin, and Lily. He delivers the line 'Quicker than falling asleep' (faithful). He shakes his head when Harry asks if Voldemort will see them, gestures to Harry's heart, says 'No. We're here, you see.' His characterisation is broadly faithful in this brief appearance. The 'grin,' the 'loping easy grace,' the 'hands in his pockets' physical detail is not filmically elaborable in the same way but the spirit is present. This scene is largely faithful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Forest scene is one of the most faithful Sirius moments in the film corpus. Some of the physical characterisation detail from the book is necessarily lost in translation to film, but the emotional content and Sirius's lines are preserved. Damage is minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Lovegood house) — Harry names Sirius when choosing the Resurrection Stone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.21: Harry says he would choose the Stone because 'we could have Sirius...Mad-Eye...Dumbledore...my parents.' Sirius is named first, reflecting his primacy among Harry's lost loved ones. The context also includes Hermione's warning that according to the tale the dead would not want to come back — which connects to the later Forest scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 15: Harry says 'Well, you could bring people back, couldn't you? Mad-Eye. Dumbledore. Sirius. Anybody.' Sirius is named third rather than first, and the order 'Mad-Eye. Dumbledore. Sirius.' subtly repositions Sirius as less primary among Harry's dead. This is a very minor ordering change.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Extremely minor. The book names Sirius first, emphasising his special place among Harry's losses; the film lists him third. The difference is marginal and does not substantially alter the scene's meaning. Included for completeness but damage is negligible.
